summary.text: Big Bang nucleosynthesis is a model for how light nuclei such as helium-4 and lithium-7 formed during the first 20 minutes of the universe.
As the expanding universe cooled, protons and neutrons combined into nuclei, and further expansion stopped the process, setting the initial cosmic abundance of these elements.
It predicts a universe of about 75% hydrogen and 25% helium-4 by mass, and refined models agree well with observations.

facts.label: Time window
facts.value: The first 20 minutes of the universe

facts.label: Predicted mix
facts.value: About 75% hydrogen and 25% helium-4 by mass

facts.label: Early pioneer
facts.value: George Gamow, a nuclear physicist, began the research

facts.label: Mass gap
facts.value: No nuclei with masses of 5 and 8 atomic mass units

facts.label: Heavier elements
facts.value: Made in appreciable amounts later, by stars

items.prompt: After nucleosynthesis ended, nearly all ordinary matter was hydrogen and helium. What kept helium-4 from feeding heavier elements?

options.label: Its nuclei hold together so strongly that they rarely break apart
Its nuclei were too light to ever collide with other nuclei
The universe stopped expanding as soon as helium formed
Its nuclei decayed back into protons almost immediately

items.explain: Helium-4 has a large binding energy, so once formed it is difficult to break apart and incorporate its constituents into heavier nuclei.

items.prompt: Where did elements heavier than lithium come from in appreciable amounts?

options.label: From fusion in the first 20 minutes of the universe
From the annihilation of electrons and positrons
From neutrons decaying after the weak interaction faded
Later, through the formation, evolution and death of stars

items.explain: Elements heavier than lithium were created at later times via stellar nucleosynthesis.

items.prompt: Early calculations in the 1940s and 50s predicted hydrogen and helium but nothing heavier. What roadblock stopped them?

options.label: Protons and neutrons refuse to combine at any temperature
No nuclei exist with masses of 5 or 8 atomic mass units to step through
The universe cooled too slowly for any reaction to occur
Too few neutrons were left once the first stars lit up

items.explain: The mass gap, with no nuclei of masses 5 and 8, meant reactions could not reach higher masses, and Fermi and Turkevich found only hydrogen and helium.

items.prompt: Why could deuterium pile up once the universe cooled below roughly 1 MeV?

options.label: Neutrons had all vanished, so nothing could split it
The universe had stopped expanding and held it together
Photons could no longer break it apart, yet fusion still ran fast
Heavier nuclei were forming faster than it could fuse

items.explain: At that temperature photon energy was too low to break apart deuterium, but the universe was still hot and dense enough for significant fusion.

items.prompt: Measurements of one light isotope in the early universe let scientists infer its density. By the 1990s, what did that density imply?

options.label: There must be mass other than baryons, later called dark matter
There must be far more stars than anyone had counted
The universe must be older than the oldest stars
There must be no helium left to measure at all

items.explain: Deuterium abundance could be used to infer primordial density, and by the 1990s that implied mass other than baryons, an idea called dark matter.

items.prompt: Before nucleosynthesis, neutrons and protons swapped identities through the weak interaction. When those swaps fell out of equilibrium, what happened to neutrons?

options.label: Most fused into helium before any decayed
Most decayed into protons, leaving about one neutron per seven protons
Most were destroyed when photons struck them
Most stayed free and made up half of all matter

items.explain: Neutrons primarily decayed to protons, and the neutron-to-proton ratio fell to around 1/7, setting the starting conditions for light nuclei.
